title: Detection as Code
summary: Detection as code is the practice of managing detection content, meaning rules, correlation logic, enrichment mappings and the tests that validate them, with the same engineering discipline applied to application source code. Detection logic lives in a version control repository rather than being clicked into a console. Changes arrive as reviewed pull requests with an author, a reviewer and a written rationale. Every rule carries structured metadata: an identifier, a description, the ATT&CK techniques it addresses, the required log sources, a severity and a documented owner. A continuous integration pipeline validates syntax against the target platform's schema, lints for required fields, checks that referenced log sources exist, executes unit tests against sample events that should and should not fire the rule, and then deploys through environments in a controlled fashion. The benefits are concrete rather than aesthetic. History answers when a detection changed, who changed it and why, which is exactly what an incident review needs. Tests catch the regression where a well-meaning edit to shared logic silently breaks unrelated rules. Portability improves because content expressed in a vendor-neutral format can be translated to several query languages instead of being rewritten by hand. The genuine difficulties are also concrete: keeping the tests' sample telemetry representative of production, handling secrets and environment-specific values without committing them, preventing repository drift from what is actually deployed in the console, and staffing the review process so that it does not simply become an approval rubber stamp. Detection as code therefore succeeds only when the pipeline and the review culture are real, not when a repository is created and left to diverge.
objectives: You will be able to explain how version control, peer review and automated validation change the lifecycle of a detection rule.
You will be able to author a rule with structured metadata that identifies its owner, required log sources, severity and ATT&CK coverage.
You will be able to write positive and negative test cases for a rule and explain why both are required to catch regressions.
You will be able to build a continuous integration check that validates rule syntax and schema before deployment.
You will be able to detect and remediate drift between the content repository and the rules actually deployed in production.
You will be able to design a review process that produces substantive feedback rather than routine approval.
